learning: If progress rises above 0.155 with max_error at or below 0.069, mass is a useful lever and the next step is a further small reduction. If max_error rises above 0.069 with progress up, the robot is drifting faster than it corrects, so the next step is a lower gain or a smaller speed increase, not a sensor change.
notes: Builder's mass 0.6 to 0.5 kg test on the iteration 5 package. The controller is unchanged so the mass effect is isolated. Steering oscillation is watched because lower inertia may raise overshoot.
rationale: The Builder's geometry sets mass to 0.5 kg. Every other field matches iteration 5: sensors at x = -0.03 to 0.03 m and y = 0.04 m, sensor_size 0.012 m, wheel_radius 0.035 m, wheel_track 0.12 m, body 0.18 x 0.12 m. Iteration 5 scored 51.01, the best so far, with progress 0.155 on the s-bend and 0.107 on the slalom and max_error at or below 0.0663 on all tracks. Across iterations 0 to 5, controller changes (kp 2.5 to 3.0, kd 0.05 to 0.1, ki 0.05 to 0.3) and sensor, lead, body and track changes each moved max_error by under about 0.007 m. Iteration 3 showed that narrowing the track and shortening the body lowered s-bend progress, so those stay fixed. I keep the iteration 5 controller unchanged (kp 3.0, ki 0.3, kd 0.1, base_speed 1.6, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], last_direction), so any change in progress or max_error is attributable to mass. Mass 0.5 kg is inside the contract range of 0.4 to 1.5 kg. Lower mass cuts yaw and linear inertia, so the robot may oscillate more. Steering oscillation has been low (0.07 to 0.16), so I do not change kp in advance. Expected result: progress rises above 0.155 on the s-bend and slalom, and max_error stays at or below about 0.069.
